HTTP Desync Attacks: Request Smuggling Reborn
intro: HTTP Request Smuggling is an advanced technique for attacking websites that have one or more front-end servers. An attack is launched by sending ambiguous HTTP requests that get interpreted as different lengths by the servers. This causes them to desynchronize, and merge requests and responses from attackers and legitimate users. This can ultimately lead to a wide range of serious effects. These include letting attackers steal plaintext passwords, and poison caches to persistently compromise critical functionality like login pages. It was first documented in 2004, but largely forgotten until we revisited it in 2019. We built on the existing request smuggling research with modern techniques and tooling, earning six figures in bug bounties along the way. We presented HTTP Desync Attacks: Request Smuggling Reborn at both Black Hat USA and DEF CON. This repopularized the technique, and has since led to a wave of discoveries and patches. In subsequent years we presented HTTP/2: The Sequel is Always Worse followed by Browser-Powered Desync Attacks. The next major installment will be HTTP/1.1 Must Die! The Desync Endgame. We also released a collection of interactive labs as part of our Web Security Academy, so you can practise applying the techniques to real systems.

intro: Template injection occurs when user input is able to define template expressions. It's commonly classified into two types. These are known as Client side template injection and Server side template injection. Client side template injection usually occurs within the browser and HTML. It happens because a developer allows user input within a webpage, and allows them to define template expressions. This then allows an attacker to inject template expressions (which are simplified JavaScript) to exploit the web application. This is similar to how Cross Site Scripting works. Some JavaScript frameworks, such as AngularJS, have a sandbox - this prevents a developer from using certain objects that they weren't supposed to. In order for an attacker to exploit this, they need to find a way to "escape" the sandbox. This means gaining access to areas such as the document object, in order to exploit the web application. intro: Somewhere in a security team's vulnerability backlog right now, a confirmed vulnerability is waiting to be fixed. Whether uncovered by a security researcher or through agentic security testing, the finding has been validated and its potential impact assessed. Yet despite security teams resolving vulnerabilities faster than ever, this one remains open, with more findings arriving every week. According to HackerOne's Security Research Report 2026, Exposure Debt: The Next Challenge in Cybersecurity, valid vulnerability reports awaiting resolution grew 131% between 2024 and 2026, even as the reports that did get fixed moved through the system more than twice as fast. So why, when the average resolution time fell from 135 days to 62 for all severities, is there such a gap between what gets found and what gets fixed? The short answer is that discovery has outrun remediation, and what it leaves behind is exposure debt, the growing gap between the vulnerabilities an organization finds and the ones it can fix. Like any debt, it compounds, with each unresolved finding extending the window in which an attacker can act. A backlog that grows 131% while resolution time falls by more than half sounds like a contradiction, but the explanation comes down to arithmetic. Part of the drop likely reflects real progress, such as tighter workflows, clearer ownership, and faster routing to engineers.

intro: CVE-2026-114924 and CVE-2026-114925 are critical vulnerabilities in Oracle E-Business Suite, Oracle’s on-premises ERP platform. CVE-2026-114924 is an authorization bypass in the Core component of Oracle Application Object Library; CVE-2026-114925 is a remote code execution flaw in the REST Services component of Oracle Applications Framework. Chained, they let a remote attacker with no credentials execute operating system commands on the EBS application tier over HTTP. Both affect supported versions 12.2.3-12.2.15 and were fixed in the Oracle Critical Security Patch Update of November 2026. Oracle rates each vulnerability 9.8 (Critical) under CVSS v3.1. Oracle’s advisory does not report exploitation in the wild, and neither CVE appears in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Horizon3 attack researchers reverse engineered the patch. Oracle Application Object Library provides the shared function-authorization layer that other E-Business Suite modules build on. CVE-2026-114924 lets crafted HTTP requests bypass those authorization checks and reach protected EBS REST functions, which run with APPS database privileges. CVE-2026-114925 is in the REST Services component of Oracle Applications Framework, where a request handler instantiates Java classes named in request input without restricting which classes are permitted — the pattern that turns a REST call into code execution on the application tier. Chaining the bypass to that handler removes the credential requirement, giving command execution as the account that runs the EBS application server. Impact: Takeover of the affected component, with High confidentiality, integrity and availability impact CVSS v3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H (9.8, Critical, scored by Oracle) Internet exposure is not required: any attacker who can reach an EBS HTTP endpoint from an internal, partner, or supplier network can attempt the chain. Oracle’s advisory publishes no workaround for either vulnerability; the November 2026 patch is the fix. Until it can be applied, restrict network access to Oracle E-Business Suite HTTP and REST endpoints with firewall rules or network segmentation. That limits who can reach the vulnerable endpoints, but it does not remove the vulnerability and does not stop an attacker who already has access to a network segment that reaches EBS. It is a workaround, not a fix.

intro: CVE-2026-132165 is a critical remote code execution vulnerability in the installer shipped with Drupal core. Under specific conditions, an attacker with no credentials can reach install.php and attempt to reinstall a running site, which can lead to site takeover or remote code execution. Some exploit paths are blocked if the web server cannot write to or change permissions on settings.php, and Drupal states that only uncommon module configurations are exploitable. Drupal rates the issue Critical at 18/25 on its own risk scale in advisory SA-CORE-2026-017; NVD has not yet published a CVSS v3.1 score. Drupal’s advisory does not report exploitation in the wild. Drupal core ships install.php, the script used to install a new site. Under specific conditions on an already-installed site, an attacker can invoke that installer and begin a reinstallation. The installation process writes configuration and runs site setup logic with the privileges of the web server, so driving it against a live site can hand an attacker administrative control of the site or code execution on the host. Drupal’s advisory notes that some exploit paths are mitigated when the web server cannot write to or change permissions on settings.php, the file that holds database credentials and site configuration. Attack vector: Network; the site’s install.php must be reachable by the attacker. Authentication: None required; Drupal states the flaw can be exploited by anonymous users. Impact: Site takeover and remote code execution; Drupal rates confidentiality and integrity impact as total. Drupal risk score: 18/25 (Critical), risk vector AC:Complex/A:None/CI:All/II:All/E:Proof/TD:Uncommon Internet exposure is not required. Any attacker who can reach a site’s install.php, including from an internal network or a staging environment, can attempt the attack. Drupal recommends blocking public access to /core/install.php in the web server configuration or in the .htaccess file in the site root, and ensuring the web server cannot write to or change permissions on settings.php. Drupal advises keeping installer access restricted after upgrading as well.

intro: Frontier AI can now find, chain and exploit vulnerabilities at machine speed. The time defenders once had between a weakness being discovered and being weaponized is collapsing. A common conclusion is that defenders are now in a waiting period. Autonomous security is coming, the argument goes, and until it arrives we hold on with the tools and tempo we have. We agree that the threat is real. We disagree that defenders have to wait. Threat actors have been learning to use and testing the capabilities of frontier models since they were released. What’s different about the abuse of ARTEX is the scale at which these new capabilities have been incorporated and turned against targeted organizations. Attackers are more comfortable with and successfully weaponizing AI powered attacks more effectively. Organizations need to leverage the same capabilities to implement trustworthy, autonomous offensive platforms to identify and fix weaknesses at machine speed and scale, then verify the fixes hold under real attacks before attackers do. The good news is the capabilities they need already exist and run safely in production today: autonomous testing that proves what an attacker can actually do in your environment. AI did not invent a new class of vulnerability or a new way to breach a company. It reduced the time and effort needed to find weaknesses, validate them, and chain them together. Attackers still do what they have always done. They find a foothold, harvest credentials, escalate privileges, and move toward what matters. What changed is how fast and how persistently they can do it, and how little expertise it now takes. That distinction matters, because a tempo problem has a different answer than a magic problem. It does not require waiting for a breakthrough. It requires defenders to operate at the same tempo.

title: The cryptography behind electronic voting (and why paper ballots are still essential)
headings: Inside the design and cryptographic safeguards of electronic voting systems
Protecting against a compromised voting client
What cryptography solves that paper ballots can’t do alone: end-to-end verifiability
We won’t be replacing paper ballots any time soon
intro: As millions of Americans vote in today’s U.S. midterms, most will use paper ballots, which are protected by strict chain-of-custody protocols and, in some cases, statistical audits. You may wonder why we still use paper for our elections and voting systems when tasks like banking, tax filing, and document signing have moved away from paper-based legacy systems and become fully electronic. The short answer: security. That may come as a surprise to some. After all, cryptography and other security advancements have enabled secure electronic systems for many applications. In fact, cryptography can be used to provide two essential safeguards in elections: keeping (1) individual votes secret while (2) making the final tally independently verifiable. This is exactly the approach of cryptographic protocols like Helios and ElectionGuard. However, Helios intentionally targets lower-risk and lower-coercion settings rather than high-stakes public elections. ElectionGuard, by contrast, is intended for public elections, but not as a replacement for a paper-based system; it is used as a cryptographic layer integrated with traditional voting infrastructure. In this blog post, we’ll explain how cryptographic techniques can help protect ballot secrecy and prevent manipulation in electronic voting systems, and explore the limitations of these systems. Although cryptography can strengthen election verifiability and have other strong security properties, it cannot fully replace the security and trust of existing paper ballot systems in general elections. The National Academy of Sciences’ excellent 2018 report on election security concludes that electronic ballot return (also known as online voting or internet voting) should not be used in general elections, since “no known technology guarantees the secrecy, security, and verifiability of a marked ballot transmitted over the Internet.” The difficulty of this problem makes sense when you consider the strong security guarantees any election system requires: Voter privacy must be maintained, even if a voter has a financial incentive to disclose their vote to a third party. Ballot integrity must be maintained. This becomes especially challenging in the electronic setting because, in general, the voter does not hold a cryptographic identity and cannot sign their ballot cryptographically. intro: Stable Linux releases lack existing security fixes because backporting them is time-consuming and often thankless work. We’re using Codex to reduce the backporting process time from days to hours per fix, empowering human patch reviewers to rapidly submit fixes for critical software like Ubuntu Long Term Support, Fedora, and the Linux kernel. By October 29, our project helped deliver fixes for 149 distinct CVEs into stable Linux kernel releases, and several fixes to Fedora and Ubuntu packages. Deploying fixes to older software requires multiple steps, including adapting fixes to older code, checking dependencies, and ensuring the fix did not introduce new bugs. A single task (like tracking down a bug in a bad commit) can take a week or more of effort that no one sees or appreciates. Our Codex workflow has reduced the human effort required to prepare and review fixes. Excluding project-specific initial setup, preparing and reviewing a straightforward backport takes about 30 minutes of human attention; a more involved case can take around three hours. The workflow’s approach is twofold: agents perform activities like identifying missing fixes, adapting patches, assembling validation evidence, running tests, and preparing submission packets, while engineers review the patches and submit them to maintainers. Those estimates only cover patch preparation and review; regression testing and maintainer acceptance remain essential. But the reduced human commitment makes a substantial class of neglected security work practical to undertake. The patch backlog is large, but we now have a practical way to work through it. Software has bugs, and we try to fix them when we can. The first place the fix happens is in the latest version of the software. Unfortunately, that’s often the only place where the fix happens. Backporting is the process of getting a fix from the latest source code to older versions. Fixes for big-name, critical bugs are indeed often backported quickly. But for many other bugs, the backporting process never happens. It is easy to understand why: software packaging is often done by volunteers who are already overworked, and backporting is frustrating, thankless work that gets little credit or publicity. For open source projects staffed by teams of volunteers, backports are (understandably) a low priority. title: Your AI agent fixed the bug, but what else did it change?
headings: patching-bugs streamlines best practices from thousands of agent sessions
The industry needs to focus on patching
intro: Today we’re publishing patching-bugs and regression-hunt, two plugins that let engineers delegate patch development and regression checks to agents. Our patching-bugs plugin reproduces reported bugs, develops fixes, and tests them. The regression-hunt plugin checks whether any changes break previously working and supported behavior. Engineers can direct the work and review their results; maintainers can supply their own security assumptions and patching requirements, so the agents work within the project’s rules. We built patching-bugs and regression-hunt through Patch the Planet, our joint initiative with OpenAI, where we’ve co-authored hundreds of security patches for widely used open-source projects. Motivated by our major successes on projects like Scapy, our plugins draw on our analysis of merged patches and thousands of our engineers’ Codex sessions. The plugins provide maintainers with a structured workflow, evidence, independent checks, and best practices to improve their patching hygiene. In our preliminary evaluations, regression-hunt produces 25% fewer false-positive findings than a baseline Codex agent prompted to “review the PR for regressions.” Our September post reported regressions introduced by some of our Patch the Planet patches. Since then, we’ve reviewed every patch that a Trail of Bits engineer authored and maintainers merged upstream. The review confirmed 21 regressions from over 130 PRs merged: 16 functional, one performance, and four build/test. None broke a security protection. (“Regression” refers to a new defect introduced by a change that breaks previously correct and supported behavior along a path a real user or attacker can reach.) For each patch, an agent looked for potential regressions, confirmed each one with a proof-of-concept (PoC) run before and after the change, and then passed the results to an engineer for review. The review was noisy: today’s bug disclosures arrive at an unprecedented speed and scale, and for patching to keep pace, the industry needs to increase its signal-to-noise ratio. The 21 confirmed regressions were identified among 58 candidates in a single run (~36% precision). But because agents take many different approaches and reach different results, each run generates more candidates to manually sort through. Standardizing both steps also makes every run repeatable and comparable. No fixed checklist will catch every regression, so we collect agent trajectories from our engineers’ patching sessions, and use the tasks that an earlier version failed to benchmark for the next one (figure 1).

intro: I tested 25 of the most popular package managers to check whether they detect a compromised package repository injecting malicious code into legitimate packages. This code integrity problem could be solved using cryptographic hashes or signatures, but many package managers are still vulnerable to this threat. Of the 25 package managers reviewed1, fewer than half used lockfiles that checked for tampering by default, and only two verified the integrity of every package they downloaded. Supply-chain attacks caused by developer compromise are a common story, but imagine what happens if ongoing mitigation attempts, including work by Trail of Bits2, are successful. If developers of popular packages are no longer the easiest targets, attackers will shift their focus to the next weakest link in the system: the package repositories that serve the code. The cryptographic answers to this problem are more subtle than they appear, and many implementations fall short due to deliberate design choices, resource prioritization, or the complexity of developer-friendly solutions. One natural answer is to include a cryptographic hash of a package’s contents in a lockfile and compare hashes after downloading the package. title: SequenceHash: multihashing for the rest of us
headings: What if I want to write my own implementation?
intro: Multihashing is one of those cryptographic tasks that’s easy not to think about too much. This is unfortunate, because multihashing is a common stumbling point when cryptographers try to use hashes. As part of our goal to “fix software, not bugs,” Trail of Bits is introducing SequenceHash and its sister function SequenceMAC, a pair of related hash constructions that bring secure multihashing to developers using hash functions other than Keccak. We hope SequenceHash and SequenceMAC will help cryptographers avoid attacks that take advantage of ambiguous input encodings. The specification is open source, and is now a part of the Community Cryptography Specification Project (C2SP). SequenceHash and SequenceMAC behave similarly to NIST’s TupleHash, but have the advantage of not being tied to a single hash function. They also don’t require developers to implement fiddly computations that aren’t byte-aligned. Instead, SequenceHash and SequenceMAC work out of the box with nearly any secure cryptographic hash function you care to use, including SHA256/384/512, BLAKE, and RIPEMD. SequenceMAC supports keys 32 bytes or longer (up to the ridiculous limit of 2128 −1 bytes). (It’s worth noting: SequenceHash and SequenceMAC rely on the security of the underlying hash for their own security. SequenceHash and SequenceMAC can’t magically make MD4 or SHA0 secure again. For the purposes of this document, it’s assumed that you have chosen a reasonable hash function like SHA256, not CRC32.) To make SequenceHash and SequenceMAC easy to use, we’re releasing three initial implementations of SequenceHash and SequenceMAC: one each in Rust, Go, and Python. We’re also releasing a large set of test vectors that cover multiple hash functions and include intermediate values to help developers debug and verify their implementations. Yeah, it’s a weird term, but the idea is pretty simple. “Multihashing” means “hashing a bunch of values together.” If you’ve ever read a cryptography paper, and there’s a step that says something like “compute the shared authenticator N=Hash(X, Y, Z, A, B),” that’s multihashing. You need to create a hash that incorporates the inputs X, Y, Z, A, and B. Unfortunately, the simple “solution” of concatenating the inputs and hashing the result can lead to serious security problems. For example, consider what happens when you hash three inputs using “raw” SHA256: Even though inputs are fed in through separate calls, they’re not separated from the perspective of the hash function—under the hood, the inputs are just concatenated.

title: Don't let TEEs break your MPC
headings: MPC: Security that depends on participant behavior
What TEEs can (and can’t) fix in MPC deployments
A cautionary tale: Rollback attacks with threshold signatures in TEEs
Best practices for combining TEEs and MPC
Layered trust beats either layer alone
intro: Threshold signature schemes, a form of multi-party computation (MPC) that lets a set of parties sign together without any one of them holding the key, are increasingly deployed inside trusted execution environments (TEEs). The combination is intended to amplify security for sensitive computations: MPC distributes trust across multiple independent parties, while TEEs root trust in the hardware manufacturer and its attestation infrastructure. But subtle issues can arise when running an MPC protocol inside a TEE without accounting for the untrusted host: for example, a malicious host could roll back the filesystem state after a threshold signer deletes a used pre-signature, causing the signer to reuse their nonce share and disclose their private key share. So is this combination worth it? Provided you treat the TEE as a defense-in-depth layer rather than a substitute for a sound protocol, the answer is yes. This blog post discusses what TEE attestation can and can’t fix in MPC deployments, explores the pitfalls we see most often in audits, and covers best practices, such as incorporating strong attestation processes and binding them to the MPC parties’ identities. Before diving into how TEEs and MPC interact, we need to understand what MPC means and what security guarantees it offers. MPC is a cryptographic technique that allows multiple parties to jointly compute a function over their private inputs without revealing those inputs to each other. The security of MPC protocols depends critically on assumptions about participant behavior. The cryptographic literature uses two primary security models: Semi-honest (honest-but-curious) security: In this model, all participants follow the protocol exactly as specified, but they may try to learn additional information from the messages they receive during the protocol execution. Participants can try to learn more than they should, but they don’t deviate from the protocol specification. Malicious security: This stronger model assumes participants may deviate arbitrarily from the protocol. A malicious participant might send incorrectly computed values, use wrong inputs, abort the protocol at strategic moments, and behave in ways designed to compromise security or learn private information. This distinction is important in the context of TEEs. If a TEE attestation can cryptographically guarantee that all parties are running the correct protocol implementation, it effectively elevates semi-honest protocols to provide malicious security guarantees (at least against certain classes of attacks, as we’ll discuss later). title: SAML: A fractal of bad design
headings: SAML and the birth of the SSO industry
intro: Born out of academia and raised in corporate IT departments, the Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) authentication protocol continues to be a staple in these organizations. However, it’s time for it to retire. With the rise of software-as-a-service (SaaS) companies in the late aughts, IT departments needed a way for users to authenticate to many new web services. SAML and the burgeoning single sign-on (SSO) industry fulfilled this need. However, SAML is being crushed under the weight of its own complexity. It’s time to deprecate it and move on to modern alternatives like OpenID Connect (OIDC). In this post, I will explore the design-by-committee origin of SAML, its progression through the ranks in academic and corporate environments, its slow disintegration at the hands of the security research community, and its (hopeful) deprecation in favor of newer protocols. What’s insidious about SAML is that it really is mostly straightforward to understand, but it’s built on a foundation of sand, bone dust, and ash; it works … if you assume XML signature validation is reliable. But XML signature validation is deeply cursed, and is so complicated that most fielded SAML implementations are wrapping libxmlsec, a gnarly C codebase nobody reads.— Thomas Ptacek, 2023 Wikipedia tells me that “SAML is an XML-based markup language for security assertions.” It was created in 2002 by the Organization for the Advancement of Structured Information Standards (OASIS) Security Services Technical Committee (SSTC). Okay, we’re not off to a great start by modern standards. XML, despite having some redeeming qualities, is quite complex compared to newer alternatives like JSON, but we’ll get more into that later. Further, a committee of subcommittees having meetings is a recipe for “kitchen-sink” protocol design (e.g., waterfall methodology, big design up front, etc.).
